articles.title: Trump’s beef import scheme wreaks havoc on fed-up red state cattle ranchers
articles.summary: Cattle ranchers in red states say Trump's 300,000 metric ton beef import plan has caused market volatility and cost them significant money per head.
articles.body: As the Trump administration desperately tries to cut costs for Americans ahead of November's midterm elections, one critical demographic to U.S. food supplies is becoming increasingly fed up. President Donald Trump in August announced that the U.S. would import 300,000 metric tons of foreign beef trim, well over half a billion pounds, from nations around the world, leaving some cattle ranchers in red states typically aligned with the president's agenda uneasy heading into a high-stakes election for Republicans. "These markets have been very volatile the last month," Greg Gunthorp, a farm-to-table cattle farmer in northeast Indiana, told Fox News Digital. "The ranchers have lost a lot of equity. The markets are down substantially." ‘WHY WOULD HE DO THIS TO US?’: TRUMP'S FOREIGN BEEF PUSH IS HURTING HIS BASE, REPUBLICANS WARN Gunthorp said the current uncertainty makes it difficult to decide whether to retain heifers for breeding or sell them as feeder cattle. Complicating matters is the fact that cattle herds in the U.S. have already thinned to their lowest level in 75 years, which could spell disaster for ranchers and consumers. Part of that shortage stems from a prolonged drought that has decimated some of the midwest herd populations. Additionally, spoking diesel costs stemming from the war in Iran means cattle ranchers are already operating on thinner margins and being forced to raise their prices. Jaclyn Wilson, a cattle rancher in western Nebraska, told Fox News Digital that how much of the 300,000 metric tons is actually imported, another unanswered question, is critical to assessing the impact that Trump administration's move will have on the industry. TRUMP WANTS CHEAPER BEEF. REPUBLICANS IN KEY RACES WARN HIS PLAN GOES TOO FAR "The only thing that really concerns me and continues to concern me, is that the market volatility is definitely there," she said. "It seems like any time that we have significant prices in the beef industry and our administration says something, we do see that market fluctuate and that can be devastating for producers that are selling calves right now or even yearling," Wilson continued. Wilson said she sold some yearling steers just after the announcement was made, and got $175 less per head than she would have normally. "And that's pretty significant for a producer," she said. Another common theme shared by ranchers who spoke with Fox News Digital is that they want the government to incentivize producing cattle, or at least stay out of the market and let cattle ranchers do it on their own. BROOKE ROLLINS, MONICA CROWLEY: AMERICA’S FAMILY FARMS HAVE KEPT US STRONG FOR 250 YEARS "You can relieve a price temporarily today, but they're not going to put cattle back in Mississippi pastures," said Mississippi cattle rancher Mary Jo Perry. "And that's the problem, is that we have a cattle shortage. So, something needs to be done to encourage farmers and incentivize them, enable them to retain heifers." Perry, who runs a grass fed, farm-to-table beef operation, said the White House's policy proposal hasn't affected her business. She sells beef to health-conscious customers who want to know that their food is high quality, and that their beef was raised without feeding on corn or soy. Wilson would just as much prefer the government to stay out the business altogether. "I think that's what's so discouraging for me as a cattle producer is I'm I'm trying to do what my family has done for generations, and somebody else is dictating it right now, she said. "I'm not given those opportunities to make that choice, and that's what's really disappointing." NEBRASKA RANCHERS STRUGGLE TO RECOVER FROM HISTORIC WILDFIRES AS DROUGHT WORSENS CRISIS "We talk about herd rebuilding, and that's something this administration is also talked about — which I agree, we do need to rebuild our cowherd — but keep the government out of it," she said. "Let it naturally happen. Mother nature, of course, is the biggest component of that." Fox News Digital spoke with Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins at the GOP Midterm Convention in Dallas last week about the cattle ranching conundrum. The Secretary said she's spoken with "hundreds and hundreds" of cattle ranchers to explain Trump's thinking in importing beef. "So, hearing from those ranchers directly was really important," Rollins said. "But what we did — and we've already done a whole lot of pro-rancher stuff a year ago — battling for private property rights, taking out the weaponization that the left had put in against our ranchers [and] working to take their land away ... so all of that was already in motion." TRUMP ADMIN SCRAPS ‘WEAPONIZED’ WILDLIFE RULE THAT BECAME 'BURDEN' ON AMERICAN FAMILIES AND BUSINESSES: BURGUM "But what that decision, as frustrated as our ranchers were, what that decision allowed was really an opportunity for us at USDA and also work across the cabinet — which, this cabinet is very unusual in that way — to put together the most pro-rancher agenda in American history," she continued. On Sept. 4, 2026, Trump signed two executive orders related to cattle ranchers and beef production. One, "Supporting America's Ranchers," is aimed at strengthening the cattle industry by ordering federal agencies to cut red tape and regulations, expand cattle grazing and look into predator management. The latter will determine whether certain species of wolves that prey on cattle have grown enough to be delisted from endangered species lists. On the same day, he signed another order focused on meat processing and market competition. It demands stricter enforcement of the Packers and Stockyards Act against unfair, deceptive or monopolistic practices in the livestock industry, along with expanding opportunities to sell meat across state lines through cooperative meat safety inspections. "President Trump has repeatedly affirmed his support for America’s great farmers and ranchers," White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told Fox News Digital. "While the Administration is addressing a short-term supply crunch in the beef market, we are simultaneously working closely with ranchers to grow America’s cattle-herd size, which is currently at a multi-decade low." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Gunthorp said the problem should have been tackled decades ago by previous administrations, but that doesn't mean trying to fix it today won't harm consumers or ranchers. "Once you fix the problem that should have been attacked 30 years ago, its gonna cause somebody pain," he said. "It's gonna cause the consumer pain [or] the rancher pain. Maybe both." Fox News Digital reached out to the USDA for further comment, but did not hear back at time of publication.

articles.title: Why are election officials in the US preparing for chaos before midterms?
articles.summary: Trump lashes out at justices who rejected his federal mail ballot plan, raising questions on his next electoral moves.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has lashed out at the Supreme Court for rejecting his push to curb mail-in voting , raising fears that the US president might use federal powers to meddle in November’s midterm elections.

“These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court,” the president lashed out after the court verdict on Monday. The justices “are merely a shell of their original selves, a court that is costing the United States Trillions of Dollars with shockingly bad rulings”.

The ruling means states can continue administering mail-in voting under their existing procedures. Mail-in and absentee ballots have been used in the United States for decades and now account for roughly a third of votes cast nationwide.

Despite the ruling, political analysts and some officials fear that Trump may not let the electoral process proceed as planned, and might pull some other strings to tilt the election in his favour.

So what voting rules exactly has Trump tried to change – and what other powers could his administration seek to use in the run-up to the midterms?

Can Trump use federal powers to tilt the elections in his favour?

Election officials across the country are concerned about the prospects of interference, from the potential for ballot seizures to voter-fraud investigations.

A Reuters investigation based on interviews with dozens of state and local election officials showed that they are adopting new strategies to prepare for political interference, misinformation, cyberattacks and intimidation tactics.

According to the report, more than a dozen local and state election officials said they are hiring outside lawyers or seeking legal training for themselves and their staff to prepare for potential demands by the administration for access to sensitive voting records or election equipment.

Nearly twice that many said they are expanding public outreach and social media campaigns to counter misinformation, including the false claims made by Trump and Republican allies that voting machines are unreliable and mail-in voting is inherently corrupt.

What have the opposition and campaigners said on Trump’s electoral agenda?

Campaigners have fiercely resisted Trump’s executive actions attempting to dictate federal voting procedures. Groups including the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) and the Brennan Center for Justice have sued the administration, arguing that the Constitution gives authority over federal elections primarily to states and Congress, rather than the president.

The pushback has also come from Capitol Hill. A bipartisan group of 261 current and former members of Congress filed a brief with the Supreme Court challenging Trump’s executive order and the subsequent Postal Service rule. They argued that the measures violated the separation of powers by taking authority over federal elections that the Constitution grants to states and Congress.

“The Constitution is clear that the states and Congress make the rules for federal elections, not the President,” Democratic Representative Jamie Raskin, one of the lawmakers leading the effort, said.

As per the US Constitution, elections are conducted by local authorities working under the states.

Raskin described Trump’s attempt to use the US Postal Service to regulate mailed ballots as “a naked power grab”, accusing the president of seeking “to inject confusion and chaos into our elections in a last-ditch effort to keep his party in power”.

Senator Alex Padilla, the top Democrat on the Senate Rules Committee, similarly argued that neither the president nor the Postal Service had the authority to determine how states administer elections. He said restricting voting by mail could particularly affect military personnel, people living in rural areas, and Americans living abroad.

The White House rejected accusations that it is seeking to interfere in the midterms, saying its measures are aimed at preventing illegal voting and ensuring confidence in the electoral system.

This is not the first time Trump has cast doubt on the security of mail-in voting, citing debunked claims of widespread election fraud associated with it. Trump falsely blamed his presidential election loss on mail-in voting fraud in 2020. Back then, he called the voting system “the greatest scam in the history of politics”. He and his supporters opposed changes made during the COVID pandemic to expand mail-in voting.

Trump and his supporters also claim that the mail-ballot plan enables a large number of non-citizens to register and vote illegally, corrupting elections. For this, he has pushed for the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act (SAVE Act) that would require citizens to provide “documentary proof” that they are American citizens when they register to vote. The legislation is stalled in the Senate over concerns that millions of voters will be disenfranchised.

Studies show that voter fraud is extremely rare. The Heritage Foundation, the conservative-leaning think tank behind Project 2025 – which inspired many Trump administration policies – documented 100 cases of noncitizens voting from 1982 to 2025. That is about 0.000008 percent of more than 1.3 billion votes cast in presidential elections during that time.

What has he done to change election rules?

Trump has been explicit about his desire to assert more federal control over the election, saying in early February that “Republicans ought to nationalise the voting”. The White House has dismissed concerns that federal actions could disrupt the midterms, arguing that the administration is enforcing election laws and safeguarding confidence in voting.

In March 2026, Trump signed an executive order directing the US Postal Service to take control of mail-in voting by designing new envelopes with special barcodes that would allow the federal government to ensure ballots are only from eligible voters.

For the midterms, that move would force all states to adopt a uniform envelope style in a short time.

The order also required states to provide the Postal Service with a list of eligible voters before elections. Several government departments, including Homeland Security and US Citizenship and Immigration Services, would also have the voters’ lists.

The postal agency was additionally empowered to deny mailed ballots if they did not comply with new standards or were not associated with registered voters on the states’ lists.

The attorney general has demanded that 47 states and Washington, DC, a federal district, hand over their complete voter registration lists, according to a tally from the Brennan Center for Justice, a nonpartisan policy group. Eleven states have complied or agreed to comply. The Trump administration has launched lawsuits against the 20 others that refused.

articles.title: Trump administration spent $9.5 billion last year on employee leave, driven by DOGE-era cuts
articles.summary: The Trump administration spent $9.5 billion last year on paid administrative leave as it pushed to cut costs, the Government Accountability Office said.
articles.body: The Trump administration spent an estimated $9.5 billion last year on paid administrative leave for federal workers as it pushed to cut costs by shrinking the government, according to a Government Accountability Office report released Tuesday. Agencies’ use of paid administrative leave jumped by 435% from 2023 to 2025, the report found, and salary costs from such leave rose sixfold. That coincides with President Donald Trump’s decision in 2025 to create the Department of Government Efficiency led by tech billionaire Elon Musk, which enacted mass firings and dissolved the U.S. Agency for International Development. Much of the increased leave cost — about $6.7 billion — came from salary paid through a DOGE-era “deferred resignation program,” GAO found. Nearly 140,000 federal employees opted into the program, according to the Office of Personnel Management. It allowed for federal workers who agreed to quit in early 2025 to still be paid through September. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the report. The GAO report emphasized that its numbers were estimates, noting that OPM “does not know the actual costs of the paid administrative leave used for workforce reduction efforts, including the deferred resignation program.” “To calculate long-term savings, OPM needs to know short-term costs of paid administrative leave used for these efforts,” the report explained. “However, OPM cannot easily and accurately do this because the paid administrative leave used for workforce reduction efforts is reported with other types of general paid administrative leave.” The deferred resignation program was unveiled just days into Trump’s second term, and federal workers received a “Fork in the Road” email laying out their options. Musk, who had quickly risen to the highest echelons of power in the administration, had previously sent an email with the same subject line to X employees, where he reshaped the company’s workforce. At the time of the program’s announcement, then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said that if federal workers “don’t want to work in the office and contribute to making America great again, then they are free to choose a different line of work, and the Trump Administration will provide a very generous payout of 8 months.” During Trump’s second term, the federal workforce has lost more than 271,000 employees as of July, according to data published by OPM. The figure includes voluntary and involuntary departures. The data indicates that between 2015, the earliest year provided, and 2025, when Trump took office again, the federal workforce grew every year.

articles.title: Move over, evangelicals: Mainline Christians are the 2026 swing voter
articles.summary: This fall, keep an eye on the Christians everyone assumed had already made up their minds.
articles.body:
For decades, election coverage has treated white evangelical Christians as the religious constituency that counts. With less than two months remaining till election day, another group deserves much closer attention: mainline Protestants.

The signs are beginning to appear in some unlikely places.

In Texas, state Rep. James Talarico (D), a Presbyterian seminarian, is the Democratic nominee for the U.S. Senate. In Kansas, Adam Hamilton (D), pastor of the largest United Methodist congregation in the country, is running for Senate in a state that has not elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century.

They are not alone. Over a dozen pastors , seminarians and former clergy have run for federal office as Democrats this year, with several winning their party’s nomination. Their faith is not window dressing. They speak about loving our neighbors, human dignity, economic fairness, pluralism and the dangers of using political power to impose one version of Christianity on everyone else.

The reaction from some conservatives has been revealing. Republican opponents have questioned whether several of these candidates are even real Christians or real pastors. One coined the term “ Pastors in Name Only .”

If faith-forward Democratic candidates are so politically irrelevant, why work so hard to discredit their faith?

The signs are also appearing in churches. This summer, the General Assembly of my denomination, the Presbyterian Church U.S.A., voted overwhelmingly to declare white Christian nationalism a “ theological error ” incompatible with the teachings of Jesus Christ.

In February, more than 2,000 people of faith joined a United Methodist-led worship service and a march around the U.S. Capitol in solidarity with immigrants. In Minnesota, at the height of the Trump administration’s deportation actions, Anoka United Church of Christ became a hub for neighbors providing groceries and supplies to immigrant families during the federal immigration surge. People who had never worshiped there began showing up to help.

Before his January 2025 inauguration, Episcopal Bishop Mariann Budde stood before President Trump and asked him, in the name of God, for mercy . Later that year, outside an Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility near Chicago, Presbyterian Pastor David Black was struck in the head with a pepper ball while quoting Jesus’s scripture .

These stories and so much more point to a revival of the mainline Church happening across our nation. White mainline Protestants make up about 13 percent of Americans , roughly the same share as white evangelical Protestants. They are hardly reliable Democratic voters. Fifty-nine percent reported voting for Trump in 2024.

But look at what has happened since. By May of this year, white mainline Protestants were evenly divided between seeing Trump as a strong leader who should be given the power he needs and seeing him as a potentially dangerous dictator whose power should be limited. Their favorable views of his handling of immigration fell from 64 percent in March 2025 to 51 percent this May. Those are the numbers of a movable constituency.

The question this election season is not whether mainline pastors can persuade conservative evangelicals to become liberals, or whether pastors running on the Democratic ticket can win over voters who disagree with them on abortion or other cultural issues. That sets the bar in the wrong place.

Millions of Christians already belong to traditions that teach them to welcome the stranger, protect the vulnerable, distrust idolatrous political power and affirm the dignity of people across lines of difference. The more interesting question is what happens when those Christians hear their own tradition speaking clearly again.

I am a Presbyterian minister. I have spent most of my adult life organizing people of faith around poverty, racism, war, immigration and democracy. Mainline membership decline is real. But decline has too often been confused with irrelevance. A church can become smaller and recover its voice.

We are seeing that in Springfield, Ohio, where people of faith are organizing in defense of their neighbors . Churches are arranging caregivers for Haitian children whose parents fear detention, delivering food to families afraid to leave their homes and helping parents prepare legal documents. Faith leaders have accompanied Haitians to ICE appointments and served communion outside an ICE office. This is Christianity practicing neighbor-love in public.

Mainline Protestants will not vote as a bloc in November. They never have. Their political independence may be precisely what makes them interesting. For years, politicians and pundits have competed for religious voters largely by asking who can win the allegiance of conservative Christians.

This fall, keep an eye on the Christians everyone assumed had already made up their minds.

Jennifer Butler is an ordained Presbyterian minister, pastor and founder and CEO of Faith in Democracy. She is the author of “Who Stole My Bible? Reclaiming Scripture as a Handbook for Resisting Tyranny” and “Born Again: The Christian Right Globalized. “

articles.title: Senate Republican on Trump claim AI threat is ‘hoax’: ‘Come on’
articles.summary: Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) on Tuesday criticized President Trump’s dismissal of rising concerns about the dangers of artificial intelligence technology. “Come on, it’s not a hoax. It’s a real thing,” Tillis, who is not running for reelection, told reporters at the Capitol. “This is something that I’ve spent a lot of my professional career in,…
articles.body:
Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) on Tuesday criticized President Trump’s dismissal of rising concerns about the dangers of artificial intelligence technology.

“Come on, it’s not a hoax. It’s a real thing,” Tillis, who is not running for reelection , told reporters at the Capitol.

“This is something that I’ve spent a lot of my professional career in, in terms of advanced technology,” he continued. “There are clearly guardrails that need to go around and anybody that told the president that this is a hoax should look at some of the things that Anthropic and some of the other leaders have seen.”

In a series of Truth Social posts Monday, Trump pushed back against calls from lawmakers and tech leaders to slow down the pace of AI development to allow time for proper safeguards and oversight practices to be implemented.

“AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX,” the president wrote in one post.

He also pointed to competition with China to develop the technology, saying “whoever wins AI wins” generally.

On Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called on AI companies to adopt several measures to “pace” the development of AI technology, including universal safety guidelines and external evaluations.

AI leaders such as Elon Musk, the CEO of xAI, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman supported Amodei’s recommendations.

“I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier,” Altman wrote on social media . “This has been a primary topic of discussions we’ve had at OpenAI in recent weeks.”

Tillis pointed to the support from within the AI community for further guardrails and oversight for the technology on Tuesday.

“Look, what CEO in the world who has a fiduciary responsibility to their shareholders would go out in public and say, ‘We need some guardrails on what we can do?’” he said.

“That by itself should invalidate any assertion that this is a hoax and something we shouldn’t be concerned with,” the senator added.

articles.title: Iran war has cost the US $38bn: How will it impact US economy, politics?
articles.summary: High energy costs at the pump and strategic setback for US in the Iran war will likely cost Trump in the midterms.
articles.body:
The United States war on Iran has cost the country $38bn so far, the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) said this week, adding that an estimated $3bn will be added every month if the conflict continues, placing strain on the country’s finances and economy.

The report, which was released on Tuesday, revealed that the protracted war is straining US munitions stockpiles and fuelling inflation as the Strait of Hormuz, a global oil export chokepoint, remains under Iranian blockade. The shortage of munitions poses a major security risk in the event of a new conflict.

The findings of the inquiry will likely add fuel to the wave of criticism about the six-month-old war , which the US launched alongside Israel on February 28, and which US President Donald Trump claimed would only last a few weeks.

The conflict has rattled the global energy market and contributed to rising prices as US voters express concern about the cost of living in the run-up to the November US midterm elections .

The CBO’s report also comes on Monday’s report from the Pentagon’s official watchdog about the losses the US has incurred throughout the war – including the first admission by the body of low weapons stockpiles.

Here’s what we know about how the war continues to affect domestic US politics, as well as its economy.

The $38bn cost cited is close to the $37.5bn shared by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at a Senate hearing on July 21.

It does not include the costs ‌of recent ⁠US strikes on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz or of Iranian attacks on US military installations in the region. Nor does it count borrowing expenses, which could add tens of billions of dollars to the total cost.

Dwindling weapons stockpiles have made up the bulk of the costs – $25bn of weapons have been used up so far – with the budget office estimating it could take five years to restore expended US stockpiles.

The conflict is likely to fuel inflation, which is expected to rise by 0.5 percentage points in the first three months of 2027, said the Congress’s nonpartisan bookkeeper.

The rising cost of the war will also act as a drag on US fiscal health as the country’s national ⁠debt topped a record $40 trillion last month.

The top Democrat on the US House of Representatives Budget Committee, Brendan Boyle of Pennsylvania, requested the inquiry into the US’s war expenditure. The Department of Defense did not cooperate with the inquiry, he said.

“Donald Trump’s disastrous war in Iran has already taken the lives of brave American servicemembers and left others wounded,” Boyle said in a statement.

How does this compare to the Pentagon watchdog’s report?

On Monday, a separate report by the Pentagon’s Office of the Inspector General also outlined US losses in the war – the first such public acknowledgement by US authorities.

That report found that the war had cost $33bn between February 28 and June 30 – with an estimated $22bn spent on expended munitions.

In a turnabout from the Trump administration’s repeated assurances that US stockpiles of weapons remain healthy, the Pentagon admitted it is indeed running out of munitions – particularly defensive systems – and is facing “bottlenecks” in supply chains.

US officials have continued to publicly reject US media reports about the shortage of munitions and missile interceptors as the war, which Trump initially said would last “four to five weeks”, has entered its seventh month. Trump has claimed that Washington has “virtually unlimited” ammunition.

The White House and Pentagon disputed the findings of the CBO on munitions shortages.

Monday’s Pentagon report also found that up to June 30, the war had caused $184m in damage to US facilities in the Gulf and killed at least 18 US military personnel.

Iranian attacks, the report said, destroyed or damaged dozens of aircraft , including at least 30 MQ-9 Reaper drones.

What has been the political opposition to the US war on Iran?

Opposition to Trump’s war on Iran is mounting, with several Republicans joining the Democrats on Tuesday to vote for a third time to end the conflict.

Seven House Republicans backed the resolution, including three voting in favour for the first time, joining all House Democrats who are opposed to the war. It will likely fail to pass in the Senate, where the Republicans hold a majority.

Even if it were to clear the Senate, Trump can still veto it.

Congress has the authority to declare war, but the president, as the commander in chief, can authorise military actions. Trump started the war before getting approval from Congress.

Past US presidents from both parties have done the same – from Democrat President Harry Truman in 1950 when sending troops to the Korean War, to Republican President Richard Nixon before the US invaded Cambodia.

Meanwhile, public approval for the war is at an all-time low. Just 31 percent of Americans support US military action against Iran, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll from late August, down from 37 percent in March.

How has the war impacted the US economy?

The most salient effect of the war for everyday Americans throughout the conflict has been soaring fuel prices. On Tuesday, the average price of a gallon of diesel in the US hit a new record high of $6.27 ($1.66 per litre), according to the American Automobile Association.

US consumers paid an additional $100bn for petrol and diesel in the first six months of the war, according to a tracker from Brown University’s Watson Institute for International and Public Affairs.

Across the country, the added cost amounts to roughly $763 per household, based on an estimated 131 million households nationwide.

Higher fuel costs are also driving up the cost of food – with the shortages of oil and gas affecting nearly every stage of the food-supply chain.

In line with his dismissive statements on dwindling weapons stockpiles, Trump has also made flippant remarks about fuel prices, telling the Reuters news agency earlier this month: “If they rise, they rise.”

Democrats have made the cost of living a key issue in the approaching midterm elections in November, which appears to have resonated with voters. The party registered wins for a number of progressives this year, from Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary to Peggy Flanagan’s Minnesota win , also in the Democratic Senate primary.

On Tuesday, several Democratic lawmakers pressed US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on the state of the economy, inflation and the rising cost of living – tying these issues to the Iran war and the rise in global oil prices. Bessent blamed inflation on the previous Biden administration and claimed Americans are better off under Trump.

The war is also affecting US fiscal health. National ⁠debt surpassed $40 trillion in August, and the 30-year treasury yield jumped to 5.32 percent that same month, the highest cost of borrowing for the US government in nearly two decades, according to the Center for American Progress.

How will the cost of the war impact the US midterm elections?

Opinion polls suggest that the Republican Party could struggle to hold onto control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate when voters go to the polls on November 3 for the midterm elections.

The rise in oil and gas prices due to the war has also become a major issue for Republicans in the lead-up to the elections.

According to a Reuters/Ipsos poll from Monday, Democrats were leading over Republicans by 44 percent to 37 percent in congressional vote preference.

On Sunday, Trump, who has promised to pay every adult $5,000 if the Republicans hold onto their majorities in both houses of Congress, said the war would end after the elections. He also shrugged off concerns that the Iran war will hamper his standing in the upcoming vote.

“I don’t believe in the word ‘regret.’ You can always question yourself a little bit,” Trump said in an interview with Fox News last week.

articles.title: Dem fundraising giant ActBlue accused of fraudulent donation 'cover-up' in explosive report
articles.summary: ActBlue allegedly weakened fraud prevention twice in 2024, with internal memos showing supervisors green-lighting donations despite red flags.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: A Democrat fundraising giant used by the biggest players on the left is being accused of covering up the acceptance of fraudulent political donations and lying to Congress about its security standards. Congressional Republicans are providing an update on their investigation of ActBlue — a platform for campaigns to raise money that's used by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, and the Democratic leaders of the House and Senate, among others — that alleges the company potentially accepted foreign contributions and concealed the evidence from the GOP's probe. ActBlue has previously denied any wrongdoing. DEM FUNDRAISING GIANT IN THE HOT SEAT AS GOP LAWMAKERS DEMAND ANSWERS OVER DODGED SUBPOENA "The Committees’ oversight has found that ActBlue, in its own words, decided to take 'a more lenient approach' to fraud prevention in 2024, weakening its fraud-prevention policies at least twice even though internal assessments showed that these changes would result in a measurable increase in fraudulent contributions," the report said, citing an ActBlue staff report. "Similarly, internal trainings directed ActBlue’s fraud prevention team to 'look for reasons to accept contributions' rather than to examine them closely for indicators of fraud — as required by federal regulation. ActBlue took this lax approach to fraud prevention even though it had detected at least 22 significant fraud campaigns on the platform in recent years, including several from foreign sources." Republicans accused ActBlue of accepting "illegal foreign political donations" and the "subsequent cover-up" of that information. As an example, the report cited a letter by ActBlue CEO Regina Wallace-Jones to Committee on House Administration Chairman Bryan Steil, R-Wis., which maintained that donations on the platform made by people with addresses outside the U.S. required a passport number for verification. KEY HOUSE COMMITTEE SCHEDULES HEARING WITH EMBATTLED ACTBLUE CEO: 'NEEDS TO COME CLEAN' But Republicans alleged that the verification "only ensures that the entered passport number contains a certain number of characters, not that it is a valid U.S. passport number," rendering it an essentially meaningless step. The report also included excerpts purporting to show ActBlue supervisors green-lighting donations despite "red flags," including a memo lauding a donation as a "great accept" but noting, "Donor sometimes has an IP in Hong Kong, but none of their other signals raise any eyebrows." Another communication appears to show an ActBlue supervisor maintaining that a denied contribution "should have been accepted." The rest of the memo stated, "It is a foreign contribution, but the name/email match, the IP/billing match, a full address with the correct country code, and there were previously accepted and successful contributions." "The donor uses an Arkansas state code, which isn’t great, but [the] system can be wonky with requiring state codes for foreign donors," the rest of the message stated. FIRST ON FOX: ACTBLUE BOARD MEMBERS IN HOT SEAT AS GOP PROBES 'SERIOUS' MISCONDUCT ALLEGATIONS An ActBlue supervisor also allegedly said a contribution "set off a lot of" alarms, but argued the donor should be given the "benefit of the doubt." The communications excerpts were included in the report and not independently verified by Fox News Digital. ACTBLUE SUES TEXAS AG KEN PAXTON, ALLEGING POLITICAL RETALIATION OVER DEMOCRATS' FUNDRAISING But despite the GOP's accusations, the report's evidence also appears to show ActBlue employees standing by the platform. An email from ActBlue employees shows they believe the company to be "the target of bad-faith political attacks at the hands of ill-intentioned operators." ActBlue also previously told the committee "there is no evidence that foreign donations through online or small-dollar contributions are a problem in U.S. elections." Despite the pushback in print, multiple ActBlue leaders who have appeared before Congress have opted to invoke the Fifth Amendment to avoid testifying. HOUSE DEM LASHES OUT AT GOP EFFORTS TO PROBE FOREIGN DONATIONS WITH STUNNING CLAIM ON MOTIVE The probe is being led by Steil alongside House Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, and House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer, R-Ky. Democrats have denounced the investigation as a cynical effort to undermine faith in U.S. elections. But Republicans argued that it's an effort to enhance that confidence by rooting out potential fraud. After we released findings of a third-party forensic analysis that completely undermined a central claim that they have made against ActBlue, Republicans are refusing to move on. Instead, they are orchestrating another political stunt before rushing out of town weeks early to go campaign." "This coordinated campaign against ActBlue isn’t about the facts, or legislating, it’s about Republicans’ efforts to silence organizations they believe threaten their agenda."

articles.title: 5 states could be the biggest losers in Trump's trade war with Canada, expert warns
articles.summary: President Donald Trump's trade war with Canada exposes $2.3 billion in Ohio exports to retaliatory tariffs ahead of the critical midterm elections.
articles.body: Americans' pocketbooks could take yet another hit ahead of the November election as President Donald Trump escalates his trade war with Canada — with five key battleground states likely facing the most fallout. Billions of dollars in U.S. exports are exposed to the northern neighbor's retaliatory tariffs that target American goods across a range of industries. The outcome? Costs are expected to continue rising for U.S. businesses and consumers in the weeks leading to the must-win midterms. Affordability remains a prominent issue for voters, while tariffs remain a cornerstone of Trump's economic agenda. He claims the strategy will result in more domestic manufacturing and pressure trade partners into agreements that are more beneficial for American industries and consumers. But the result so far has been an increase in prices for the average American family. "American manufacturers or American businesses who rely on Canadian inputs are going to start to feel the pain right in the lead up to going to the ballot box," David Clement, policy director of the free market nonprofit Consumer Choice Center, told Fox News Digital. TRUMP JUST EXPANDED HIS TARIFF PLAYBOOK WITH A POWERFUL TRADE WEAPON NO PRESIDENT HAS EVER USED Clement identified Ohio, Illinois, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin as among the states most exposed to negative fallout, based on their current trade with Canada and the goods targeted by the tariffs. "Ohio is by far the most vulnerable state in terms of exposure from the Canadian retaliatory tariffs," Clement said, estimating roughly $2.3 billion in exports to Canada are exposed. He pointed to machinery, transportation products, minerals and metals as major sources of that vulnerability. In Michigan, the impact is particularly evident in the auto industry, where supply chains are deeply intertwined with neighboring Ontario. "Most Americans don’t know that a single component on a U.S.-assembled vehicle can cross the border upwards of eight times before it’s actually completed," Clement said. "When you are tariffing automotive parts going across the border each way," he added, "it really gums up the very intertwined supply chain for cars between Michigan and Ontario." A FRESH MIDTERM HEADACHE FOR THE GOP JUST HIT A NATIONAL RECORD Those costs can eventually make their way to consumers, Clement argued. Pennsylvania also faces significant exposure. Clement said about 25% of the state's exports go to Canada, much of it machinery and equipment, putting just under $1.8 billion in exports at risk. What the trade fight means politically is less certain. Clement argued that even a change in congressional control after November would not necessarily bring the tariffs to an end. A POPULAR COCKTAIL HAS A TRUMP TRADE PROBLEM YOU PROBABLY DIDN’T KNOW ABOUT "The idea that Canadian retaliatory tariffs are going to swing the midterms in the Democrats’ favor and then all of a sudden create an end to the trade war is a fantasy," Clement said. He cited the legislative hurdles to reversing presidential trade policy and noted that the Biden administration kept a number of tariffs imposed during Trump's first term. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Still, Clement argued the timing could matter, with Canada's retaliatory tariffs already in place as the midterms approach. "Cost of living, cost of goods, cost of doing business is such an important factor for Americans who are going to be casting a ballot," he said.

articles.title: ‘Worse than Watergate’ New FBI files detail agent’s push to join Trump probe, investigate Elon Musk
articles.summary: Chuck Grassley released FBI emails from Crossfire Hurricane, calling Obama and Biden administration operations against Trump worse than Watergate.
articles.body: An FBI agent repeatedly sought to join the bureau's Russia investigation involving President Donald Trump, while another pushed for a criminal investigation of Elon Musk over an email asking federal employees what they accomplished at work, according to documents newly released by Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa. The records span internal FBI communications from 2017 and 2025, covering both the bureau's Russia investigation and a proposal to investigate Musk. Grassley said the exchanges reflected political bias within the bureau and showed the "Deep State" working against Trump. The documents were released as part of a broader batch involving Crossfire Hurricane and other FBI matters. "The previous Democrat administrations under Obama and Biden conducted secret, insidious and downright evil operations that almost took down our government," Grassley said during an Oversight hearing with FBI Director Kash Patel. "That's arguably worse than Watergate." Crossfire Hurricane was the FBI's 2016 counterintelligence investigation into whether members of Donald Trump's presidential campaign coordinated with Russia's election interference, though Special Counsel Robert Mueller's investigation did not establish a criminal conspiracy between the campaign and the Russian government. DAN BONGINO REVEALS HE FOUND 'MOTHER LODE' OF SECRET RUSSIAGATE FILES INSIDE FBI BURN BAGS Over the past decade, the Senate Judiciary Committee, at the direction of Grassley, has released several rounds of documents from a few FBI operations such as Operation Arctic Frost and Round River, alleging that the Justice Department was being weaponized against Trump and Republicans. "The overall sustained efforts by the Deep State in the dark corners of the bureaucracy is worse than anything Trump has been accused of. At least he’s upfront and open so people can judge," Grassley said. At the center of the Senate Judiciary Committee's most recent document release are three former FBI agents: Kevin Gounaud, Walter Giardina, who was fired by Patel in August over accusations of political weaponization, and Timothy Thibault. Gounaud, who left the bureau in February, according to his LinkedIn, sent an email in February 2025 seeking to begin a criminal investigation of Musk. At the time, Musk was a special government employee overseeing DOGE. Gounaud's complaint centered on Musk announcing on X his plan to have all government employees share five things they worked on that day. "Musk used a non government system (twitter) to relate information that allegedly was for official purposes. In doing so, because he is monetized (he is a majority owner of twitter) he likely generated income for himself based on Twitter's monetization model and/or advertising revenues," Gounaud wrote. "His use of twitter in this and other instances is conceptually similar to Hillary Clinton's misuse of a private email server for government business." Grassley later criticized the former FBI agent in a post on X. JACK SMITH'S SENATE PHONE RECORDS PROBE TURNS TO VERIZON'S HANDLING OF SUBPOENAS "Here is an email I released 2day showing an FBI agent who was ready2 open a CRIMINAL CASE all bc Elon Musk asked govt bureaucrats 2 report 5 things they did in a wk," Grassley wrote. "Compare that 2 Iowans who work frm sunup to sundown EVERY DAY Washington rlly is an island surrounded by reality." The document dump also shows that Giardina emailed at least seven times over the course of four weeks beginning in January 2017 asking to be assigned to Crossfire Hurricane. The findings of the investigation were handed off to special counsel Robert Mueller a few months later in May. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER The emails show that Giardina was in correspondence with Thibault, who Grassley accused of violating the Hatch Act. The allegation stemmed from Thibault resharing a post on Twitter by the Lincoln Project, which called Trump a "psychologically broken, embittered, and deeply unhappy man." The U.S. Office of Special Counsel (OSC) opened an investigation into Thibault, but before the investigation ended he retired from the FBI in August 2022. In January 2024, the U.S. of Special Counsel determined Thibault did violate the Hatch Act with his retweet, but only issued a warning letter and closed the case. Thibault is included in several emails sent by Giardina to former Supervising Agent Joe Pientka. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Based on the records known to date, that case didn’t advance," Grassley said. "His efforts, as well as the case he tried to open on Senator Sinema, undercut public statements by former FBI officials that agents don’t get to pick their cases." Fox News Digital reached out to the FBI for comment.

articles.title: Sunny, Barack Obama's 'fiery and gorgeous' dog, dies
articles.summary: The Portuguese Water Dog spent 13 years with the family, meeting many high-profile visitors in the White House, including Pope Francis.
articles.body:
The Obamas' beloved pet dog Sunny has died after 13 years with the family, Barack Obama has announced.

"Yesterday, we lost a cherished member of our family," the former US president wrote on X, describing her as a loyal dog who was "pretty much perfect" and always by their side.

The family had two Portuguese Water Dogs in the White House. They got Sunny at the beginning of Obama's second presidential term in 2013.

Sunny met many high-profile visitors while Obama was president, from foreign dignitaries to Pope Francis.

Their other dog, Bo, joined the family in 2009 as a gift for daughters Sasha and Malia to help them settle into the White House. Bo died in 2021.

Obama said that when Sunny joined the family they "immediately fell in love".

He described her as "full of boundless energy", saying she leapt over the hedges on the South Lawn like they weren't even there.

Sunny most enjoyed "having us run around with her, roll on the floor with her, or have her belly rubbed for as long as we were willing", he wrote.

"She loved the girls, even if they were pestering her when she was napping. She loved our team, and would often follow them around, helping them on the job."

Obama added that Sunny was "a loud and sloppy drinker" who hated getting wet.

"For thirteen years, she would be by our side – always loyal, always sweet, always ready for adventure, still fiery and gorgeous till the very end of her days."

He said the family would miss her terribly and that she was now with her "big brother" Bo.

Sunny was a regular at White House events, meeting children at Christmas parties and international dignitaries on state visits. In 2015, Sunny and Bo met Pope Francis in the Blue Room at the presidential residence.

Former chief White House photographer Pete Souza said it was an "honour" to work with Sunny, describing her as a "willing subject" who had "the rare distinction of being petted by both a President and a Pope".

There is a long tradition of pets at the White House. Donald Trump is believed to be the only president in the past 100 years to not have a pet.

articles.title: Abolish extended Senate debate? The ends do not justify the means.
articles.summary: Senior legal fellow Thomas Jipping argues that President Trump’s push to abolish extended debate via the nuclear option threatens the Senate’s traditional role as a check on government power and risks permanent partisan instability.
articles.body:
President Trump is demanding that Senate Republicans abolish extended debate, the Senate’s most distinctive feature for more than 200 years, to pass certain legislation, including the SAVE Act. Extended debate is an important limit on government power. Abolishing it would permanently weaken the Senate and its unique role in the legislative process to gain a few temporary political objectives. The ends truly do not justify the means.

It’s tempting to say, at least when it’s to your advantage, that the majority should always get everything it wants, especially when, like today, the same party controls Congress and occupies the White House. America’s Founders saw it differently. They knew that protecting our liberty — the primary purpose of government — requires structuring government the right way for the long term. There need to be “controls” on government and loosening those controls undermines liberty.

Those controls include separating government power into three branches, and dividing Congress into two differently designed houses. The Founders designed the Senate to be more deliberative than the action-oriented House and, therefore, senators have long had more freedom than House members to debate legislation.

In the beginning, the consensus was that debate should focus on the legislation at hand. Starting in the 1830s, however, senators increasingly used their freedom to debate not to facilitate the legislative process but to disrupt it. A filibuster occurs when senators refuse to stop debate so the Senate can vote on a bill.

Still, during the 19th century, the Senate repeatedly refused to abolish extended debate altogether. Instead, starting in 1917 , the Senate regulated extended debate with rules that set a specific vote threshold (60 votes today) for invoking cloture, or ending debate, on legislation.

My own analysis , just published by Advancing American Freedom, documents how both parties have used extended debate to their advantage when in the minority. Republicans, for example, have stopped dozens of significant Democratic initiatives that would have empowered labor unions, federalized elections, restricted election-related speech, liberalized immigration, addressed climate change, and even prohibited pro-life state or local laws. If ending debate required 51 votes rather than 60, as some of the loudest voices demand, much of that radical legislation would be law today.

The Senate has amended the cloture rule a few times, adjusting the vote threshold or the legislative matters that the rule covers, but always through the established process and with wide bipartisan support. The Senate has regulated extended debate, but has never abandoned it completely.

Doing so would be disastrous, especially because the only way to do it during this congressional session would be to bypass the established amendment process and guarantee endless partisan retaliation.

The regular amendment process won’t work this time because it requires 67 votes for cloture on a proposed rules change. The alternative is a parliamentary maneuver called the “nuclear option” that would leave the words of the cloture rule intact but pretend that they mean something different. The Senate, no doubt by a slim party-line margin, would vote that the words “three-fifths” in the cloture rule actually mean “simple majority.” If you are thinking that 60 does not, in fact, equal 51, you are right. But “whatever means necessary” includes pretending.

Rigging the rules in this way, so that any partisan majority can get whatever it wants, would create all sorts of long-term problems.

Let’s say the SAVE Act, requiring proof of citizenship to register for, and vote in, federal elections, is on the books and, when they next control Congress and the White House, Democrats set out to repeal it. With extended debate, Republicans could stop them; without it, they cannot.

Senate control has changed partisan hands no fewer than 10 times since the Senate first adopted its cloture rule. Neither party has held control of both the legislative and executive branches for more than four years since 1969.

Partisan control is going to change hands. If the Senate becomes like the House by abolishing extended debate, a slim partisan majority will have no obstacle to getting everything it wants, including undoing whatever was done when the opposing party had control. That is a plus if power is more important, but dangerous if liberty is the priority.

Wanting to get our way all the time is human nature and, as James Madison asked in 1788 : “[W]hat is government itself, but the greatest of all reflections on human nature.” If winning is everything, too much power is likely to end up in too few hands. That’s what the Founders designed our system of government to prevent.

In April 2017, 61 senators signed a letter to the party leaders defending “the right of Members to engage in extended debate on legislation before the United States Senate.” They noted “the unique role the Senate plays in the legislative process” and urged opposition to “any effort to curtail the existing rights and prerogatives of Senators to engage in full, robust, and extended debate as we consider legislation.” Twenty-seven of those signers, 15 Democrats and 12 Republicans, serve in the Senate today. They were right then and should stick to that position now.

Thomas Jipping is senior legal fellow at Advancing American Freedom .

articles.title: House cuts week short, will leave DC on Wednesday
articles.summary: House GOP leaders have cut short the final legislative week before the midterm elections, announcing that lawmakers will leave Washington after Wednesday’s votes. The announcement, from the office of Rep. Tom Emmer (Minn.), the GOP whip, shortens the week by a day. A vote scheduled for Thursday, related to California environmental rules, has been moved…
articles.body:
House GOP leaders have cut short the final legislative week before the midterm elections, announcing that lawmakers will leave Washington after Wednesday’s votes.

The announcement, from the office of Rep. Tom Emmer (Minn.), the GOP whip, shortens the week by a day. A vote scheduled for Thursday, related to California environmental rules, has been moved up to Wednesday.

The move not only allows lawmakers to head home early for the campaign trail, but it also means that lawmakers will not be forced to take a vote on impeaching Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth before the elections.

Sponsored by Rep. Tom Massie (R-Ky.), the eight impeachment articles accuse Hegseth of conducting an illegal war with Iran, because it lacks congressional approval, and killing suspected drug smugglers without judicial oversight, among other charges. Massie introduced the resolution on Tuesday as a privileged motion, which requires a floor vote within two legislative days, setting a deadline of Thursday had the chamber remained in session.

The next time the House will be back in session after Wednesday will be Nov. 9, following the midterm elections. Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) earlier this month canceled the last two weeks of the September session, despite House Democrats urging him to keep the House in session to implement bipartisan AI safeguards.

Johnson had defended the abbreviated schedule on Tuesday, telling reporters that much of the legislative work is stalled in the Senate. The upper chamber has yet to pass a budget resolution for a third reconciliation package, legislation that would reauthorize food and agricultural programs for the next five years and a cryptocurrency regulation bill dubbed the Clarity Act – all major GOP priorities.

“Right now, it almost feels like a pointless exercise for us to continue sending and stacking legislation over there, when members could be in their districts campaigning in this very fateful moment,” Johnson said. “That’s a critically important thing.”

Johnson said that he’s sent every House member notice that if the Senate begins to move on legislation, he will bring “everybody back and we’ll get it all going.”

articles.title: 2 Iowa GOP reps support Iran war powers resolution for first time
articles.summary: Two Iowa Republicans backed a war powers resolution in the House over the conflict in Iran for the first time, a notable move for two members from the deep-red Hawkeye State as the midterms near. On Tuesday, the House passed a Democratic-backed war powers resolution with an aim to restrict President Trump’s military actions in…
articles.body:
Two Iowa Republicans backed a war powers resolution in the House over the conflict in Iran for the first time, a notable move for two members from the deep-red Hawkeye State as the midterms near.

On Tuesday, the House passed a Democratic-backed war powers resolution with an aim to restrict President Trump’s military actions in Iran, the third time the lower chamber has passed such a measure.

The House voted 220-204 in favor of the resolution, with seven Republicans throwing their support behind it, including Reps. Thomas Massie (Ky.), Brian Fitzpatrick (Pa.), Warren Davidson (Ohio), Tom Barrett (Mich.), Mariannette Miller-Meeks (Iowa), Zach Nunn (Iowa) and Nancy Mace (S.C.).

In a post on the social platform X Tuesday night , Nunn said that “Iran must be held accountable for killing Americans, supporting terrorism, threatening the Strait of Hormuz, and pursuing nuclear weapons.”

“Iowa has already paid a devastating price, including two service members killed by an Iranian drone in Kuwait. Congress owes them, their families, and every American in uniform clear objectives and constitutional oversight,” he added in his post.

Miller-Meeks also made a post on X , writing “I said it in March: the mission had to stay focused and limited, because Americans do not want another forever war,” and that “I will not vote to keep our soldiers in an open-ended war, with Iowans paying too much at the pump.”

Both Miller-Meeks and Nunn’s move in favor of a war powers resolution comes shortly before the Iran war reaches its seventh month. The conflict has proven unpopular among the American public and driven up energy costs as the Strait of Hormuz has been closed.

The two Iowa lawmakers are also facing strong challenges from Democrats in their districts, with nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report placing both of their races in the “toss up” category.

articles.title: House to leave early, punting Hegseth impeachment vote until after November elections
articles.summary: House lawmakers will leave early for the November midterm elections after Republican leaders canceled votes for Thursday.
articles.body: House lawmakers will leave Washington on Wednesday night for the last time before the November midterm elections, after GOP leaders said they were canceling votes set for Thursday. The change in schedule means that the House won’t vote on Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky’s resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth until after Election Day. GOP leaders insisted their decision had nothing to do with Massie’s impeachment efforts. But they were eager to avoid a difficult vote for many of their vulnerable Republican members who have been uneasy with Hegseth’s leadership during the unpopular six-month war with Iran. Talking to reporters Wednesday, Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., slammed the Massie impeachment effort as “ridiculous” and defended Hegseth. “It’s a publicity stunt by someone who wants attention. It will immediately be tabled, of course. ... We’ll probably do it when we come back, but it’s a stunt,” Johnson said (tabling would effectively kill the measure). “Secretary Hegseth has done an extraordinary job, the Department of War. We’re in the middle of international conflicts right now, and we should not be playing games with national security.” Massie filed his resolution to impeach Hegseth as “privileged” on Tuesday, meaning the House would need to act on it within two legislative days. That set up a vote no later than Thursday, but then GOP leaders scrapped votes that day, pushing the impeachment vote until after the election. The House is slated to return to Washington on Nov. 9. Meanwhile, the Senate will remain in session for the next three weeks. Johnson, who is fighting to preserve his razor-thin GOP majority, said he wanted his members to return home and get back on the campaign trail. “It’s time for our members to go home to their districts and make their case to the American people, to go and explain all the great things we’ve done. You’ve seen the record. You’ve seen what we’ve delivered ... the largest middle- and working-class tax cut in U.S. history. We have the violent crime rate at a 126-year low,” Johnson said. It’s “an extraordinary record of achievement,” he added, “and so I’m excited for my Republican colleagues to go home and talk to the American people, work in their districts, and explain to them not only serving their constituents but explaining to them all the great things we’ve done for them and all the things we’re going to do in the days ahead.” Massie, who has served in Congress since 2012, has clashed repeatedly with House GOP leaders, President Donald Trump and Hegseth over the Iran war. The congressman voted for multiple Iran war powers resolutions to restrict Trump’s military operations in Iran and Venezuela. Last year, Trump and his political team recruited former Navy SEAL Ed Gallrein to run against Massie in the GOP primary in Kentucky. In an unusual move, Hegseth campaigned for Gallrein one day before the May primary election. Massie lost. On Tuesday, with no advance warning, Massie took to the House floor and began reading his impeachment resolution. Hegseth “has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution, if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law,” Massie said.

articles.title: Trump should follow Jefferson’s lead and step back from media lawsuits
articles.summary: Deep down, Donald Trump seems convinced the news industry is his enemy — and he wants to punish them.
articles.body:
President Trump’s recent Oval Office outburst against CNN reporter Kristen Holmes was just another in a long string of Trumpian media confrontations. The president repeatedly ordered Holmes to “be quiet” as she tried to ask him questions during a White House gaggle. Of course, Trump told Holmes that her employer represents “fake news.”

Trump followed up that clash with a social media outburst against NBC’s Kristen Welker, calling for Welker to be punished by the Federal Communications Commission. Welker claimed Trump’s record on primary endorsements “had some mixed results.” As Trump pointed out, his endorsement scorecard is actually better than “mixed,” but that is beside the point. Welker has First Amendment protection to characterize Trump’s record however she wants, and the FCC knows better than to try to punish a broadcast journalist for editorial commentary, even if it is questionable.

Deep down, Trump seems convinced the news industry is his enemy, and he has repeatedly made that sentiment known. He distrusts journalists and wants to punish them.

A case can be made that many news outlets are, indeed, biased against Trump. CNN, The New York Times, and the big three broadcast networks have well-earned the president’s ire. Studies from the Media Research Center, right-leaning as it is, confirm the establishment media’s unbalanced coverage of MAGA and Trump. But again, that is beside the point. The broad constitutional protection of a free press allows news outlets to act unprofessionally and even play fast and loose with the facts.

Trump is hardly the only president to hate the press. Even staunch First Amendment supporter Thomas Jefferson accused the news industry of “demoralizing licentiousness” and “abuses” during his second inaugural address . Jefferson even urged citizens to ignore the newspapers of that time because they engaged in “false opinions in league with false facts.”

Past presidents battled the media largely from their White House bully pulpits. But Trump has taken his running feud beyond the jawboning stage and into the courtroom; his tenure in politics has been punctuated by an unprecedented string of lawsuits against news outlets and journalists. He has targeted The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, CNN and even the British Broadcasting Corporation, among others, seeking billions of dollars in damages.

The prospects of Trump winning these lawsuits are quite thin, mostly because of the actual malice standard. That ill-defined notion means courts have to basically psychoanalyze journalists and a newsroom culture, and then conclude that any false reporting about a public official was done with specific intent to defame. The Supreme Court established that standard in 1964’s New York Times v. Sullivan case , when it sought specifically to allow robust coverage of public figures who, presumably, have plenty of avenues available to correct any reporting errors.

Trump’s $3.8 billion defamation lawsuit against The Washington Post was dismissed earlier this summer by a federal judge precisely because Trump’s lawyers had failed to produce “convincing evidence of actual malice.”

Sure, Trump has won settlements in a couple of his legal skirmishes, collecting $15 million from ABC and another $16 million from CBS . Some observers believe ABC and CBS would have prevailed in court, but merely caved and offered relatively small settlements just to make the lawsuits go away .

Given that Trump and his lawyers surely know he can’t really win lawsuits by challenging journalistic content, such as it is, it is clear the motivation is just to make news organizations miserable. News outlets have to devote time and big money to defend themselves. Further, Trump’s lawsuits do generate a certain amount of news coverage in which Trump criticizes journalists. And the cage-rattling plays well to the Trump base.

The news industry, for its part, shows no sign of minimizing its negative coverage of all things Trump. The potential for more lawsuits has hardly caused the NYT, MS NOW or CNN to be less aggressive in criticizing the president and his administration. Thus, the ongoing litigations and threat of more lawsuits has not created a “chilling effect” on the journalism industry.

Trump would be wise to follow the second-term strategy of his White House predecessor, Thomas Jefferson. The Sage of Monticello said unfair journalists should be “left to find their punishment in the public indignation,” because “public duties more urgent press on the time of public servants.” Trump has plenty of public duties that need his attention in the last two and a half years of his presidency, without continuing to swat at the gnats of the press corps .

Jeffrey M. McCall is a media critic and professor of communication at DePauw University. He has worked as a radio news director, a newspaper reporter and as a political media consultant.

Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) is working with Christian groups to push Republican officeholders and candidates to sign a “Declaration for Life” pledge to fight for legislation to restrict abortion.

Hawley announced the pledge after hosting the first Missouri Prayer Breakfast with dozens of pastors in the historic Kennedy Caucus Room in the Russell Senate Office Building.

“This is a declaration for life for life, calling on the country to once again embrace a culture of life and in particular to put a stop to the scourge of the abortion drug known as mifepristone,” Hawley announced after the prayer breakfast.

The declaration was drafted by more than 30 pastors from around the nation and signed by more than 100 pastors from Missouri and 50,000 citizens to coincide with the nation’s 250th anniversary.

“We think that this declaration written by pastors calling on spiritual leaders and everyday Christians across America to stand for life and to confront the scourge of chemical abortion is so critical on this 250th anniversary,” Hawley said.

Tony Perkins, the president of the Family Research Council, a leading national Christian public policy ministry, and Sean Feucht, a Christian singer and founder of the Let Us Worship movement, joined Hawley in unveiling the pledge.

Perkins, a longtime Christian leader, declared the Republican Party has “lost its voice” on “life” issues.

“Unfortunately the Republican Party has lost its voice on the life issue and in that vacuum there are leaders that are stepping forward like Sen. Hawley calling upon the church, communities and the country to step up on behalf of the unborn,” he said. “I’ve seen the movement on the life issue, we’ve made great progress but there’s been a tremendous setback.

“I think we’ve reached the point where we have to call upon the faith community, the pastors, Christian pastors, to step into this vacuum and speak unequivocally about the sanctity of human life and hold elected officials accountable to a standard. This is a starting point of establishing a standard for what we should be aspiring to as a nation,” he added, thanking Hawley for his leadership.

Perkins pointed out that the Republican National Committee removed its call for a national abortion ban from its official party platform in the summer of 2024.

Hawley introduced legislation in March to ban the use of mifepristone for abortions and to give women the power to sue the drug’s manufacturers. His bill would withdraw the Food and Drug Administration’s approval of mifepristone for abortion and make distribution and labeling of the drug for ending pregnancies a violation of the federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act.

Hawley’s mifepristone bill has at least seven Republican co-sponsors but hasn’t received much discussion within the Senate GOP conference since he introduced it.

“My observation is that when it comes to elected officials in Congress that there hasn’t been much will to do much of anything to protect the innocent and unborn and I think we’ve got to change that. And one of the things we want to do with this declaration for life is to call on candidates for office in both parties to sign this declaration to say … we support protecting human life in law … and we support putting an end to chemical abortion,” Hawley said.

“I think that we should call on anybody who wants to serve in this body to take that pledge and that commitment,” he said.

Advocates for lower taxation led by Grover Norquist, the president for Americans for Tax Reform, made great progress in the 1990s and early 2000s in pushing Republican candidates to sign the Taxpayer Protection Pledge to promise not to vote for tax increases.

Hawley and Christian leaders envision the “Declaration for Life” becoming a similar tool to hold Republican officeholders to account on abortion-related votes, such as restricting mifepristone and stopping federal funding of Planned Parenthood, which provides family planning and abortion services.

“We’re just going to put it out there, pastors have drafted it, we have handed it out to all of these pastors, Missouri pastors behind me today, many of whom have already signed it,” he said. “We’ll just put it out there and ask candidates … to support this and commit to this.”

Perkins, who heads one of the biggest Christian political advocacy groups in the country, said that “pro-life groups will circulate this as a standard because the Republican Party platform removed the life provisions in the last platform.”

“That’s where the Republicans lost their voice on the life issue. In that vacuum, this is a very clear statement as Sen. Hawley said. It’s been put together by pastors,” he said. “Our organization, we will be putting it out there. We will help make this a standard for candidates to commit to a pro-life position.”

The four-page declaration states “the defense of human life is the oldest of American causes” and that the right to life heralded in the Declaration of Independence is the “most foundational of all rights.”

The declaration points out that the Supreme Court’s reversal of Roe v. Wade in 2022, which overturned the national right to an abortion, did not end abortion in America and that more abortions are being performed today because of the widespread availability of mifepristone.

“So long as the abortion drug can turn every mailbox in America into an abortion clinic, state laws alone cannot protect human life. We need a national response,” it states. “As such, we call on Congress to end the scourge of mail-order abortions by banning the abortion drug.”

articles.title: AI 'doomers' risk kneecapping US vs China, but ex-Pentagon vet says both extremes miss the mark
articles.summary: Will Thibeau, a former Pentagon AI official, warns that "doomer"-driven AI regulation could hand China an edge and entrench an OpenAI-Anthropic duopoly.
articles.body: "Doomer"-driven AI regulation could kneecap the U.S. against China while helping tech giants lock in their lead over smaller startups, a former Pentagon AI official who also worked for AI company Palantir Technologies told Fox News Digital. The warning follows the resignation of an Anthropic researcher who said increasingly powerful AI could threaten humanity, while President Donald Trump called fears of rogue AI a "hoax" and compared those advancing such warnings to climate-change alarmists whose predictions, he argued, haven't come true. "The notion that I think the president and I share is that we should let the race play out, that the risk of global extinction is not real, it is in fact a hoax," Will Thibeau, a former Palantir deployment strategist who later worked in the Pentagon’s Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office, told Fox News Digital. TRUMP UNLOADS ON TECH TITANS PUSHING FOR SLOWDOWN ON EMERGING INDUSTRY: ‘WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!’ "The stakes of losing to China, of losing the opportunity to transform our economy, are so high that we shouldn't let 'doomerism' define public policy," the retired Army Ranger added. Thibeau’s position is not that Washington should take a hands-off approach to AI, but that the U.S. should race aggressively at the frontier while narrowly addressing concrete risks — threading the needle between denying China an advantage and preventing regulations backed by today’s leading AI firms from entrenching a "duopoly" at the expense of new American innovators. "We must maintain an edge at the frontier, so our economy has the license on the first benefits of artificial intelligence. Enhanced manufacturing capabilities, enhanced processing power, decision-making in financial markets," he said, disputing the idea that Beijing will not race full bore because the technology could countervail the CCP’s grip by incidentally empowering civilians. "Artificial intelligence has the potential to redefine our economy and transform the country for the good," Thibeau said, while rejecting both predictions that it will make life "unrecognizable" and that it poses an uncontrollable "extinction" risk. MORNING GLORY: SPARE US THE AI APOCALYPSE RHETORIC. LET CONGRESS DECIDE WHAT COMES NEXT Those "hyperventilating" over either extreme, he argued, miss the "clearly defined middle path" for AI development. Thibeau said some of AI’s most important applications are military, where it can process battlefield data quickly enough to give U.S. forces an advantage while helping preserve civilian life. BATTLEFIELD ROBOTS OPEN NEW FRONT IN INNOVATION WAR WITH MAJOR US ADVERSARY "I’m very bullish, if you will, on how artificial intelligence can be applied for the military," he said. While Thibeau said fears of "drone swarms run amok" are not realistic, he acknowledged AI carries real risks that policymakers should address without allowing those concerns to justify sweeping rules that slow U.S. development or undermine its military edge. The larger danger, he argued, is that leading AI firms can absorb regulations that smaller newcomers cannot. "There is a duopoly, perhaps a triopoly if you include Google," Thibeau said, naming Anthropic and OpenAI as the two companies clearly in the lead. ANTHROPIC CEO CALLS ON AI INDUSTRY TO SLOW DOWN TECH RACE, DRAWING SUPPORT FROM ELON MUSK, SAM ALTMAN "They want to slow the game so they can use their built-in advantages and their current lead to solidify this market dominance… to make it harder for new entrants to rise the market chain [and capture] the regulatory incentives of the government." Fox News Digital reached out to all three firms for comment. ANTHROPIC CEO LIKENS AI FIGHT WITH CHINA TO COLD WAR, SEEKS 'DISARMAMENT NEGOTIATIONS' Anthropic policy documents outline concerns about biological risks, cyber risks, loss of control, and the automation of research and development while also underlining that regulations must "protect innovation." In terms of government oversight, Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., told reporters Tuesday that AI should be the rare time for bipartisan collaboration on regulation. OBAMA PRIVATELY SOUNDS ALARM ON ‘DANGEROUS’ AI, URGES DEMOCRATS TO PUT ISSUE AT CENTER OF AGENDA "If there's ever a time for Republicans to break from their blinded allegiance to Trump, it is now. The world is in danger and Republicans are on the sidelines sucking their thumbs," he claimed. Former Vice President Kamala Harris added in a statement that AI is "advancing at an alarming speed," and signaled she sides with the Big Tech firms calling for pacing the "frontier" — which Thibeau warned about. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "A slowdown is critical in order to ensure AI serves the public interest," she said in part of a lengthy statement. Meanwhile, House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., said guardrails are necessary for the AI sphere but that Congress should not respond with a heavy hand. "We have to put up some guardrails, some safety measures in place to ensure that AI doesn’t run away… But at the same time, we’ve got to make sure that we don’t lose our edge in the global competition on this with China," he told NBC News.
