articles.title: Republicans came back to Washington and made voting harder
articles.summary: House Republicans introduced a non-binding resolution calling for the enactment of the SAVE America Act upon returning to Washington after the August recess.
articles.body:
After five weeks with no floor activity, House Republicans kicked off their return to Washington following August recess by pushing a non-binding resolution calling yet again for enactment of the SAVE America Act.

Even for President Trump’s Republican Party, that is remarkably tone deaf.

For five weeks, House Republicans were back home hearing from their constituents about the affordability crisis in America and the most corrupt administration in our nation’s history. They heard from families struggling with grocery bills, housing costs and everyday expenses. And then returned to Washington and made one of their priorities a non-binding resolution calling for enactment of a bill that has already passed the House.

It is embarrassing to even write that sentence. That is how determined Republicans seem to be to make Congress irrelevant.

And let’s remember what the so-called “SAVE America Act” really is.

A bill that would make it harder for married women and veterans to vote.

A bill that would essentially gut mail and online voter registration.

A bill that would force states to hand over voter rolls to Trump’s Department of Homeland Security.

That is what House Republicans chose to spend their time on.

Perhaps I should not be surprised. As costs skyrocket, Republicans are afraid to face their constituents at the ballot box. Instead of changing course or addressing the problems families are facing, they are making it harder for Americans to vote. They want bills like the SAVE America Act to disrupt election administration and keep millions of eligible voters away from the polls.

President Trump has issued illegal executive orders aimed at blocking ballot access for millions of Americans, including an unlawful attempt to weaponize the U.S. Postal Service and eviscerate vote-by-mail systems in states across the country. His administration has defunded and gutted the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and its support for election administrators. And the president and his allies continue to spread misinformation and disinformation about the integrity of our elections.

House Democrats will continue to fight back. Because despite these continued efforts by the president and his allies, our elections are safe and secure. State and local election administrators, not the president, run elections across the country. They know their communities and their systems, and they do the hard work every day to make sure eligible Americans can vote and their votes are counted. The courts have also continued to reject unlawful attempts by the Department of Justice to force states to turn over their voter rolls. As of earlier this month, the department’s record in those cases stood at 0-23 .

House Democrats’ objectives are straightforward: every eligible American must have a meaningful opportunity to cast a ballot, and those ballots must be counted fairly and accurately.

A recent poll found the Republican Congress with a 15 percent approval rating. Fifteen percent of the American people approve of the job Congress is doing. Some might understandably think that number is low. After watching exercises like this, I am surprised it’s that high.

Would this symbolic resolution do anything to lower gas prices? Would this messaging bill make groceries cheaper? Would it do anything to hold the crooks in the White House accountable? The answer is simple: it would not.

Americans sent us here to solve our nation’s problems. They did not send us here to spend our time finding new ways to make it harder for them to vote.

Promises were made to the American people. They have not been kept. The American people deserve better than this.

Joe Morelle represents New York’s 25th District in Congress and is ranking member of the House Administration Committee

articles.title: War crimes court turns 'blind eye' to top world threats while targeting Americans, Trump admin accuses
articles.summary: The State Department accused the International Criminal Court of targeting Americans while ignoring atrocities by Iran, North Korea and Syria.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: The Trump administration is escalating its campaign against the International Criminal Court (ICC), accusing the Hague-based tribunal of ignoring atrocities committed by authoritarian regimes while unlawfully targeting the U.S. and its service members. State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott told Fox News Digital that the ICC has "violated international law by targeting the United States and American servicemen" while it has "repeatedly turned a blind eye to the abuses of despotic regimes that fund terrorism, brutally suppress and torture their citizens, and carry out crimes against humanity." The remarks are the latest step in the administration's broader effort to weaken the court, which U.S. officials argue has exceeded its authority by investigating Americans despite the U.S. never joining the Rome Statute that established the ICC. Earlier this year, the administration imposed sanctions on senior ICC officials and pledged to continue a diplomatic campaign against the tribunal. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SANCTIONS SITTING PRESIDENT OF THE INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL COURT FOR 'ABUSES OF POWER' Pigott vowed the U.S. "will continue its diplomatic campaign to systematically dismantle the court." The administration has already imposed sanctions on ICC officials and launched a diplomatic campaign urging allies to reject the court's authority and reconsider their membership in the Rome Statute. The department argued the ICC has never opened a preliminary examination into Iran despite decades of allegations of human rights abuses, including the suppression of protests, executions of political prisoners and state sponsorship of terrorism. It also noted that the court closed a preliminary examination into North Korea without opening a full investigation and has not pursued further action despite a 2014 U.N. report documenting crimes against humanity. It also criticized the court's handling of ISIS and Syria, arguing the tribunal has failed to pursue accountability despite documented atrocities committed by the terror group and the Assad regime. The ICC's authority is limited by the Rome Statute that created the court. Iran, North Korea and Syria are not parties to the treaty, meaning the court generally cannot prosecute crimes committed on their territory unless another jurisdictional basis exists or the U.N. Security Council refers the situation. Security Council efforts involving Syria have previously been blocked by Russian and Chinese vetoes. The administration argues those jurisdictional limitations do not excuse what it describes as the court's willingness to pursue Americans. ICC PROSECUTOR WHOSE NETANYAHU WARRANT FUELED MAMDANI ARREST THREAT IS FIRED OVER SEXUAL MISCONDUCT According to the State Department, the ICC "engaged in jurisdictional overreach" by investigating alleged actions by U.S. personnel in Afghanistan even though the U.S. is not a party to the Rome Statute. The ICC could not immediately be reached for comment. In 2020, the court authorized an investigation into alleged war crimes committed during the war in Afghanistan, including by Taliban fighters, Afghan security forces and U.S. military personnel and CIA officers. The investigation examined allegations that some U.S. personnel committed torture, cruel treatment and other abuses in Afghanistan, as well as at CIA "black sites" in Poland, Romania and Lithuania, all of which are parties to the Rome Statute. Because those alleged crimes occurred on the territory of ICC member states, prosecutors argued the court had jurisdiction even though the U.S. is not a member. The CIA's black-site program emerged after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks and involved the secret detention and interrogation of terrorism suspects at clandestine facilities overseas. A 2014 Senate Intelligence Committee report detailed the program, describing the use of so-called "enhanced interrogation techniques," including waterboarding, and concluded the methods were more brutal than previously acknowledged and did not produce unique, otherwise unobtainable intelligence. The report also described secret detention facilities in countries including Afghanistan, Poland, Romania and Lithuania. WORLD COURT PROSECUTOR WHO WENT AFTER NETANYAHU FOR WAR CRIMES SUSPENDED OVER SEXUAL MISCONDUCT The latest criticism comes amid one of the most contentious periods in the relationship between Washington and the Hague-based court. The U.S. has long objected to the ICC's investigation into alleged war crimes committed by U.S. personnel in Afghanistan, arguing the court lacks jurisdiction over Americans because the U.S. is not a party to the Rome Statute. The dispute intensified further after the ICC issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity related to the war in Gaza, a move the U.S. rejected as illegitimate. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Since returning to office, the Trump administration has made confronting the ICC a central foreign policy priority, imposing sanctions on multiple judges, prosecutors and other officials while vowing to dismantle what Secretary of State Marco Rubio has described as a "fatally politicized" institution that threatens U.S. and allied sovereignty.

articles.title: Prominent Dem’s fatal error prompts Republican to predict ‘red tidal wave’ in blue stronghold
articles.summary: Eric Flores calls James Talarico's reversal on gender surgery and "God is nonbinary" comments proof that Texas Democrats lack a record to run on.
articles.body: Despite widespread predictions of major Democratic electoral victories this November, South Texas GOP candidate Eric Flores is predicting a "red tidal wave" in the Lone Star State, with controversial Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico as the most prominent Democrat at the top of the ticket. Flores, a U.S. Army veteran running in Texas' 34th Congressional District, called out Talarico for his recent "flip-flop" on some of his most controversial stances, including calling God "nonbinary" and saying there are six sexes. He argued that Talarico’s decision to walk back those statements is proof that he and other Democrats in the state "don’t have a record to run on." In an interview with Fox News last week, Talarico said he supports banning gender surgery for minors and opposed transgender-identifying men competing in women’s sports. He also addressed his controversial "God is non-binary" comment, saying, "I was being provocative with that statement. I get that," and "what I was trying to say is that you can't use human categories to define God, and that's not controversial theologically. In fact, the late Charlie Kirk, the late Pope Benedict, all said the same thing." In response, Flores shot back, "Those aren't provocative statements; those were statements that were made with intention, and that's showing who he truly is." TALARICO SAYS HE 'MISSED THE MARK' AS HE BACKTRACKS ON CONTROVERSIAL WOKE STATEMENTS Flores is running in a competitive race for a heavily Hispanic district that has long been a Democratic stronghold. The seat is currently held by Rep. Vicente Gonzalez, D-Texas. Despite long being considered a solidly blue district, President Donald Trump won it in 2024. Republicans have also narrowed Democrats’ advantage in the district over the past several election cycles. Flores argued that, with Talarico as the most prominent Democrat running statewide in Texas, this will be the year the GOP finally seals the deal. "They're saying that there's a blue wave. Well, I got news for folks, there's a red tidal wave coming because we're going to be getting rid of the wrong type of Democrats like my opponent," he said. He credits the GOP’s rising chances in the district to eroding trust in Democrats in South Texas. He said, "the voters are finally asking the questions that South Texas deserves to hear." "Everything that I hear throughout Texas 34 is simple, and they are thinking about their pocketbook; they're thinking about inflation and the cost of living," he explained. Flores’ pitch to try to break through the Democrats’ longtime hold on South Texas is "that this isn't a contract election, it's a contrast election." "What does that mean? That it's common sense, which is the Republican Party, against communism and fake and the wrong type of Democrats like my opponent who are voting 80 to 85% of the time with AOC," he said. THE HISPANIC VOTE IS UP FOR GRABS IN 2026. CANDIDATES WHO IGNORE IT WILL LOSE In response, Gonzalez told Fox News Digital that "Eric Flores is a rubber-stamp intellectual lightweight that can’t think for himself. He will continue to support the Iran war and policies that raise the cost of living for hardworking South Texans. All while shamelessly taking his ‘Trump Endorsement’ language off all his political ads and sending fundraising messages asking for donors to help him pay back his personal primary campaign debt instead of trying to win his race." "That should certainly feel like an air of confidence to the party," Gonzalez continued, adding, "Trust me, he’s not fooling Democrats or Republicans for that matter. And it won’t be long before he’s back representing child molesters in South Texas." Fox News Digital is not aware of any evidence that Flores represented child molesters in his capacity as either a private practice attorney or assistant U.S. attorney. Fox News Digital also reached out to Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., for comment. Regarding Talarico’s Fox interview, Flores said, "They're asking him, do you really think that there are six genders? Do you really support these gender surgeries against minors? That's the same thing with Talarico and my opponent, when they get questioned, all they can do is flip-flop because they actually don't have a record to run on other than this far-left woke DEI agenda." A spokesperson for Talarico’s campaign directed Fox News Digital back to comments he made during his interview last week. Fox News spoke with Talarico at a food drive campaign event in Dallas on Tuesday. Talarico’s event took place as the first-ever GOP midterm convention kicked off just miles away in downtown Dallas. Asked whether he would vote as a U.S. senator in favor of a national ban on gender surgery for minors, Talarico answered, "Absolutely." He said, "I've been consistent on this issue," explaining his opposition to a Texas bill to ban transgender surgeries on minors by saying the measure "was overly broad." "If you go back and check, I voted for a major amendment to limit the bill to banning surgeries for minors," he said. "As a lawmaker, my job is to try to sift through everything the bill does. And sometimes there's stuff in it that's really harmful, and I have no choice but to oppose the bill as a whole." In 2023, as a member of the Texas House of Representatives, Talarico voted against Senate Bill 14, which prohibited certain gender surgeries, puberty blockers and certain hormone treatments for minors. Democrats proposed 18 amendments to the bill, all of which Talarico supported and all of which ultimately failed. EXCLUSIVE VIDEO: DEMS FACE MAJOR DEFEAT AFTER PARTY ‘MISSED THE CUE’ IN TOP TARGETED DISTRICT: CANDIDATE "It's why I try to use amendments, to narrow the focus of the bill so that it does exactly what we intend it to do," he continued. "It's what I tried to do with that piece of legislation, and unfortunately, the amendment I supported was unsuccessful." Talarico also told Fox News, "I supported amendments that would have given the power to make these decisions to local communities," adding, "like conservatives used to believe, I believe in local control." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In the same interview, Talarico acknowledged that men in women’s sports is a significant issue in Texas. He said, "I oppose trans athletes playing in girls’ sports if it endangers safety or fairness." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "Every sport has to be safe and fair. As a former public school teacher, I care a lot about our student athletes. I care a lot about our students. And so, I will oppose trans athletes playing in girls’ sports if it risks safety or fairness," he said. Comparing himself to his Republican opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, Talarico said, "I am proud of my legislative track record delivering for Texans. I brought Democrats and Republicans together to pass 60 bipartisan bills that lower people’s costs and get the economy back on track. I'll put my record up against Ken Paxton’s every day of the week and twice on Sunday."

articles.summary: Presented by SourceAmerica — Plus: 🗳️Trump campaigns with Whatley in North Carolina {beacon} It’s Wednesday, or Hump Day since the Geico camel commercials have returned 🐪 (“Uh oh…Guess what day it is?”). In today’s issue: Federal Reserve expected to raise rates Senate Republicans plan spending cuts Trump to campaign with Whatley Kash Patel strikes back…
articles.body:
It’s Wednesday, or Hump Day since the Geico camel commercials have returned 🐪 (“Uh oh…Guess what day it is?”).

Programming note: We’re Joshua Feldstein and Abigail Walker , filling in for Cate today. Please send us your tips, comments and story ideas to jfeldstein@thehill.com and awalker@thehill.com.

House GOP leaders have made the call to cancel Thursday’s votes, starting recess a day early. We won’t be seeing members back in Washington, D.C., until after the midterms.

Democrats had urged House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) to keep the House in session to work on legislation around artificial intelligence (AI) safety.

Rep. George Whitesides (D-Calif.) said Monday that “we need to have a safety stand-down with AI for at least one month for all companies.” However, Johnson and Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) have dismissed calls for a urgent response or hefty regulations.

Looming Hegseth vote : The weekslong House recess means members won’t have to vote on Rep. Thomas Massie’s (R-Ky.) move to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth until after November’s election.

Once Massie introduced the impeachment resolution on Tuesday, it initiated a 48-hour clock for a vote to be called to the House floor.

Johnson said Wednesday the resolution would have been quickly tabled — effectively putting Massie’s motion on hold.

But that still would have required Republicans to go on the record with a politically sensitive vote related to the divisive Pentagon chief and unpopular Iran war.

With the House now out until Nov. 9, after Johnson canceled the last two weeks of September sessions earlier this month, that’s a later problem.

“Oh, let me talk about the impeachment vote. That’s ridiculous. It’s a publicity stunt by someone who wants attention,” Johnson told reporters.

“Secretary Hegseth has done an extraordinary job at the Department of War. We’re in the middle of international conflicts right now, and we should not be playing games with national security.”

Trump’s allies in the Senate are setting up to slash tens of billions of dollars in federal spending following the midterm elections.

The Hill’s Alexander Bolton : Thune announced Tuesday the Senate would not move on a reconciliation package until after the election on Nov. 3.

It will likely be necessary for Republicans to move emergency defense funding to help cover the costs of the Iran war and a boost to the Pentagon’s base budget through the regular appropriations process. Trump also wants to raise the debt limit by about $5 trillion to extend the nation’s borrowing authority through the end of his term.

Those priorities will be really expensive, and getting 51 GOP senators on board will likely require some big offsets.

“Inflation is a problem. We all understand the cost of living is a problem. The only way we’re going to get the cost of living down is if we balance the budget,” Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) said about the proposed cuts.

“We’ve basically come to the realization if we want some fiscal controls, that’s the point in time to do it, so we need to be in favor of a debt limit and offer those types of fiscal controls,” said Senate Budget Committee Chair Ron Johnson (R-Wis.). “That’s initially what reconciliation was for, deficit reduction.”

President Trump is heading to North Carolina Wednesday evening to campaign with GOP Senate nominee Michael Whatley , looking to give him a boost in an uphill battle.

According to recent polls, Whatley is currently trailing former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper (D) by double digits. Trump has won the battleground state three times and looks to deliver a jump in the polls for the GOP, according to The Hill’s Julia Manchester.

What’s the strategy?: Convince Trump supporters the president is effectively on the ballot, even though he’s not. It’s a message Trump hammered during the Republicans’ midterm convention in Dallas last week.

“He [Trump] helps Michael Whatley in trying to energize the Republican base, which is something Republicans have to do,” said Paul Shumaker , a North Carolina-based GOP strategist.

President Trump has long pined for lowered interest rates and selected Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh to make it happen.

But it doesn’t appear the president will get his way. Investors are all but certain that the Fed will raise interest rates by a quarter point at its meeting today, with an announcement coming at 2 p.m.

A Reuters survey of economists earlier this week found that roughly 85 percent expect rates to go up. Heather Long, a chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, wrote Friday, “A September Fed rate hike is almost locked in now.”

“It’s the right call,” Long continued in her post on X. “The risks are growing that inflation remains entrenched (or keeps broadening). Fed Chair Warsh doesn’t want to make the same mistake Powell did of waiting too long to hike.”

articles.body:
Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) on Tuesday ruled out launching a 2028 presidential bid , with less than 18 months before the Iowa caucuses.

“I have no intention of doing so, period,” Hawley told the Washington Examiner .

The Missouri Republican, whose term ends in 2031, has occupied a populist lane within the GOP, calling for strict antitrust enforcement against large corporations and backing labor unions — while maintaining socially conservative views on issues such as abortion .

“No antitrust exemptions for AI [artificial intelligence]. Not a chance,” Hawley wrote Tuesday on social platform X.

Vice President Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio lead the lion’s share of early polls of the Republican field, although neither have announced a run.

Vance said in June that he will discuss a presidential run with his wife, second lady Usha Vance, after the November midterms. The two welcomed their fourth child in July.

“The way I make decisions is, I try not to make them until I absolutely must,” the vice president told host Robert Costa on “ CBS Sunday Morning .”

Rubio, who unsuccessfully sought the GOP presidential nomination in 2016, also told RCN last week he has “ no plans ” to run as of now

“I’m not a candidate for anything right now, and I’m 100 percent focused on my job,” the secretary of state said in Spanish.

Some of Hawley’s Senate GOP colleagues have expressed interest in running , including Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), and libertarian Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.), both of whom also ran in 2016.’

Regarding the 2028 presidential race, Hawley told the Examiner he had “no insight to offer” on the matter.

“I don’t know who will run or what will happen. We need to get through these elections first,” he added, referring to the midterms .

The senator, though, had one warning for 2028 GOP contenders: Do not ignore religious conservatives.

“You cannot win anything without them. You cannot win a primary without them. You cannot win a general election without them,” he told the outlet, putting evangelical Protestants, conservative Catholics and conservative Orthodox Jews in that bloc.

“So, I’d be real careful about trying to marginalize that coalition,” Hawley added later.

articles.title: The Inflation Reduction Act’s broken promise is still costing patients
articles.summary: Critics argue that the Inflation Reduction Act is increasing costs and reducing patient access to medications through price negotiations and Medicare Part D restructuring.
articles.body:
When President Biden signed the Inflation Reduction Act into law, his administration promised it would make prescription drugs more affordable and accessible for seniors.

A recent analysis found that nearly one in four initial attempts by patients to fill a prescription for one of the first drugs selected for Medicare’s drug price negotiation program was rejected. Patients relying on immunology and oncology treatments felt this even more intensely, with rejection rates climbing as high as 59 percent and 67 percent, respectively.

The lesson from the Inflation Reduction Act and other countries around the world is simple: Government drug price controls do not improve patient access. In many cases, price controls create incentives to ration care and empower government bureaucrats at the expense of patients and the development of new therapies.

That dynamic is playing out across Medicare Part D, which has undergone a significant overhaul over the past several years.

According to the Congressional Budget Office, the Inflation Reduction Act increased taxpayer costs while also jacking up premiums for consumers and out-of-pocket costs for many patients. While the law caps seniors’ annual out-of-pocket costs at $2,100 this year, other dynamics are shifting fixed dollar co-payments per prescription to percentage-based fees tied to the cost of the drug. Because most seniors have drug costs less than $2,000, many are paying more out of pocket.

The law also required new mandatory manufacturer discounts, shifted billions of dollars in financial responsibility from Medicare to private Part D plans, and completely redesigned how prescription drug benefits are provided. This tripled the financial risk borne by plans, which are now raising premiums on consumers or exiting the market entirely.

Rather than fixing the problem, the Biden administration launched a temporary Part D Premium Stabilization Demonstration, spending billions of taxpayer dollars to help some of the country’s largest health insurers keep premiums artificially low. This did not address the structural flaws created by the Inflation Reduction Act; it simply delayed them.

The Trump administration is ending the demonstration at the end of the year . With billions in temporary taxpayer support going away, the full impact on 2027 premiums will soon become clearer. What is already apparent is that the Inflation Reduction Act didn’t reduce costs; it simply shifted them throughout the Medicare program.

By requiring plans and manufacturers to shoulder significantly more of the cost of expensive medicines, the redesign also risks weakening incentives to innovate by creating greater uncertainty about whether companies can recoup the significant time and resources required to develop new treatments. At the same time, plans facing greater financial liability have stronger incentives to manage their formularies more aggressively, potentially limiting patient access to cutting-edge therapies.

Now, career bureaucrats at the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services are considering a policy that could further reduce patient access to innovation. The Inflation Reduction Act defined a “Qualifying Single Source Drug” as a product family, not a single product, essentially allowing bureaucrats the latitude to include as many drugs as possible into their price controls. Under the proposal, these bureaucrats could group separate drugs that have each received their own FDA approval simply because they share the same active ingredient and subject them to Medicare price negotiation on the same timeline, even when the newer medicine represents a meaningful improvement over the original.

These follow-on innovations require years of additional research and new clinical trials, often making treatments safer, more effective, or easier for patients to receive.

Treating these advancements as if they were the same drug would reduce incentives to invest in the kinds of improvements that make a real difference for patients.

Patients with multiple myeloma, for example, previously spent hours receiving an IV infusion of Darzalex . Thanks to continued innovation, many patients can now receive Darzalex Faspro, a quick subcutaneous injection administered in only minutes. That improvement required additional research, clinical trials, and FDA approval, but it has made treatment far more convenient for patients.

Under Medicare’s proposal, innovators could have less reason to pursue similar advances if meaningful improvements are treated no differently than the original medicine for purposes of Medicare price negotiation. Over time, patients could lose out on the next generation of treatments that make medicines safer, more effective and easier to use.

This harmful law is already disrupting the market and driving up costs. Career bureaucrats shouldn’t use the law to worsen its impact by further limiting patient access to care and future medical innovation.

Joel White is the president of the Council for Affordable Health Coverage. He previously served as staff director of the House Ways and Means Committee. Hannah Anderson is the senior director of policy for the Center for a Healthy America at AFPI and the former deputy chief of staff for the Department of Health and Human Services .

articles.title: Kansas’s former GOP governor backs Democrat over Marshall for Senate
articles.summary: Former Kansas Gov. Bill Graves (R) on Tuesday endorsed Adam Hamilton, a Democrat challenging Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall (R). Saying the country is “facing increasing partisan gridlock and division,” Graves said it is “time Kansas does something different” and elect Hamilton, a Methodist minister. “For the last six years, Senator Roger Marshall has turned his…
articles.body:
Former Kansas Gov. Bill Graves (R) on Tuesday endorsed Adam Hamilton, a Democrat challenging Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall (R).

Saying the country is “facing increasing partisan gridlock and division,” Graves said it is “time Kansas does something different” and elect Hamilton, a Methodist minister.

“For the last six years, Senator Roger Marshall has turned his back on Kansas,” the former governor remarked in a video Hamilton shared to social platform X. “In contrast, Adam Hamilton stands as a bulwark of kindness, humility and service to others.

“It is for those reasons, and many more, that I believe Kansas should send Adam Hamilton to the U.S. Senate.”

The Hill has reached out to a spokesperson for the National Republican Senatorial Committee for comment.

Graves, 73, led the state from 1995-2003. Prior to that, he spent eight years as Kansas’s secretary of state.

This is not the first time Graves has endorsed a Democrat for statewide office. In 2018 and 2022 , he backed Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly (D) over her GOP opponents, with Kelly winning both times.

Hamilton, the senior pastor of the Church of the Resurrection, is trying to become the first Democrat to win a Senate race in the Sunflower State since former Sen. George McGill in 1932. To do so, he will have to defeat Marshall, an obstetrician in his first term in the upper chamber.

The election handicapper Cook Political Report rates the race as “likely” to go Republican. The Hill’s polling partner, Decision Desk HQ , also gave Marshall a roughly 8 in 10 chance of beating Hamilton as of Monday.

As of the end of June, Marshall’s campaign held a financial edge over that of his Democratic opponent. The Republican had nearly $5.4 million on hand to less than $1.8 million for Hamilton, according to the Federal Election Commission.

articles.title: Former Renault-Nissan chief Ghosn skips corruption trial in Paris
articles.summary: Former car executive Carlos Ghosn, who faces charges of corruption and influence-peddling in France, did not appear in court in Paris at the start of his tri...
articles.body:
Former auto executive Carlos Ghosn did not appear in court in Paris at the start of his trial on corruption and influence-peddling charges, with allegations of paying €900,000 to former French Culture Minister Rachida Dati between 2010 and 2012.

Ghosn, who fled to Lebanon, faces up to 10 years in prison and heavy fines, while Dati took her place in the dock at the beginning of the trial.

The court is considering whether to proceed with the trial in Ghosn's absence or to adjourn, with the decision pending and Ghosn claiming he did not receive the summons in time.

Former car executive Carlos Ghosn, who faces charges of corruption and influence-peddling in France, did not appear in court in Paris at the start of his trial on Wednesday.

No lawyer appeared in court on behalf of the 72-year-old, who has fled to Lebanon, where he holds citizenship.

The former Renault-Nissan chief is accused of having paid €900,000 ($1 million) to the co-defendant, former French culture minister Rachida Dati between 2010 and 2012. The funds came from a Dutch subsidiary of the Renault-Nissan Alliance.

It is suspected that the payments may be linked to lobbying activities on behalf of the car manufacturer in the European Parliament. At the time, Dati was a lawmaker in the European Parliament.

Investigators have charged Ghosn with abuse of power and corruption, and Dati with accepting bribes. Both have denied the allegations. They face up to 10 years' imprisonment and heavy fines. Dati took her place in the dock at the start of the trial.

In court, the parties to the proceedings discussed whether the trial should go ahead in Ghosn's absence or be adjourned. Ghosn had requested an adjournment in a letter from his solicitors, claiming he had not received the summons to the trial in good time.

Lawyers representing anti-corruption organizations involved in the proceedings, as well as the prosecution, have demanded Ghosn be tried in absentia. A decision by the court, which was also considering separating the proceedings against Ghosn, was still pending.

The architect of the Franco-Japanese automotive alliance Renault-Nissan-Mitsubishi was detained and charged in Tokyo on November 19, 2018 for breaches of stock exchange regulations.

In April 2019, he was released on bail from pre-trial detention subject to strict conditions. Ghosn then made a daring escape at the end of December, hidden in a box on a private jet via Turkey to Beirut.

Ghosn has repeatedly denied the allegations against him in Japan and accused the French authorities of a witch-hunt. He sees himself as the victim of a conspiracy to prevent Nissan from forming closer ties with Renault. Lebanon does not extradite its citizens.

articles.title: GOP lawmakers blindsided by new revelations about Trump Butler shooter: 'Awfully strange'
articles.summary: Thomas Matthew Crooks' father searched for ways to block his son's gun access months before the Butler, Pennsylvania, assassination attempt on Trump.
articles.body: Republican lawmakers were apparently blindsided this week by new documents about Thomas Matthew Crooks, the 20-year-old who attempted to assassinate President Donald Trump and was subsequently shot dead. Crooks opened fire on Trump during a campaign rally in Butler, Pa., in July 2024. A bullet grazed the then-candidate’s ear, while a rally attendee was killed as he attempted to shield his family. "During our piece that we were working on, none of the federal agencies were working with us at all. They were going to work on their own, and they told us, ‘We're going to do ours, and then we'll get back to you.’ So this is two years later. Nobody's gotten back to us," Rep. Mike Kelly, R-Pa., who chaired a bipartisan House task force aimed at investigating the shooting, told Fox News. "That's under the former administration. So everything that's under the executive branch at that time, under the Biden administration, we had no access to information at that time," he said. Kelly also said the House task force's Dec. 10, 2024, report was written largely with input from local authorities and little from the federal level. COLE ALLEN CLUES PILE UP AS THOMAS CROOKS’ SECRETS DIED WITH HIM — EXPERTS CITE EVIDENCE GAPS IN TRUMP ATTACKS "It's awfully strange that all the questions we asked, 'We'll have to get back to you on that.' And we have very limited time, as you know, to actually get to what we wanted to. So when we finished our report, it was basically based on everything that we could gather from local law enforcement, hardly anything from the feds at that time," Kelly said. Fox News Digital reviewed the documents in question and found that Crooks’ father, Matthew Crooks, had searched for ways to prevent his son from accessing firearms in May 2024, roughly two months before he clambered up a rooftop in his attempt to assassinate Trump. A source familiar with the task force’s work told Fox News Digital that the May 2024 search by Matthew Crooks was not known to House lawmakers during their investigation. TWO YEARS AFTER BUTLER, THREATS AGAINST TRUMP KEEP ASSASSINATION ATTEMPT IN SHARP FOCUS "The Task Force report corroborates that Matthew Crooks handed Thomas Crooks the rifle used in the assassination attempt on July 13, 2024," the source said. Kelly’s spokesman told Fox News Digital that his office was not aware of federal authorities interviewing Crooks’ family. 3 SECRET SERVICE OFFICIALS UNDER INTERNAL INVESTIGATION FOR POTENTIAL MISCONDUCT The records were obtained by Senate Judiciary Chair Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, as part of his ongoing inquiry into the Butler assassination attempt. So far, the records turned over to the Senate show Thomas’ actions were a surprise to his family, and his motive is still a mystery. Members of the Senate Judiciary Committee told Fox News Digital that they had yet to see the FBI documents, but argued that it was reason enough that the full details of that day in July 2024 needed to be brought to light. Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., a member of the panel, told Fox News Digital that the documents dump is "something that should have happened," but there was still "so much that we don't know about what happened." "I think we have got to, I've been saying forever now, we have got to have a full accounting of everything that happened on that day, all of the failures, law enforcement failures that occurred," Hawley said. I WAS AT BUTLER TWO YEARS AGO WHEN AMERICA SAW WHAT COURAGE LOOKS LIKE When asked about Crooks’ father trying to stop him from getting access to guns, Hawley said, "This gets back to if this guy was out there, if he was, if he was displaying erratic behavior, was that reported?" He recalled being on the ground days after the attempt. Hawley described how easily he could’ve gotten onto the rooftop from where Crooks fired off rounds toward the stage and charged that there was "no coordination" among the several local and federal law enforcement agencies present that day. "I mean, this is just wild. And I still don't think we've gotten a full accounting," Hawley said. "Pretty much everything we know about this is from whistleblowers. You know, we need a full accounting of what really happened on that day." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Listen, otherwise, we run the risk of things like this happening again. And we run the risk of it turning into a, you know, JFK situation where, all of these years later, we still don't really know what happened," he continued. "We owe it to the American people to figure out what exactly happened and what we need to fix. Clearly, there were massive failures."

articles.title: Massie says House GOP leaving to avoid Hegseth impeachment vote
articles.summary: GOP Rep. Thomas Massie (Ky.) accused House Republican leadership on Wednesday of sending lawmakers home early to avoid a vote on his resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The announcement, shared by the office of GOP Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.), cuts the final legislative week before the midterm elections short by one day. “And…
articles.body:
GOP Rep. Thomas Massie (Ky.) accused House Republican leadership on Wednesday of sending lawmakers home early to avoid a vote on his resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

The announcement, shared by the office of GOP Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.), cuts the final legislative week before the midterm elections short by one day.

“And there it is. Just as I predicted,” Massie wrote in a social media post . “They’re canceling Congress tomorrow to avoid the vote on IMPEACHING @SecWar.”

The Kentucky Republican added that this decision will “make it harder” to reach the required votes needed to pass a bipartisan discharge petition on follow-up legislation to the Epstein Files Transparency Act, which was passed by the chamber last year.

Massie said the measure, which he co-sponsored with Democratic Rep. Ro Khanna (Calif.), had around 190 of the 218 signatures needed to pass on Tuesday evening.

On Tuesday, Massie introduced eight impeachment articles against Hegseth, accusing the secretary of conducting an illegal war against Iran and killing suspected drug smugglers without proper oversight, among other charges.

The GOP lawmaker told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins on Tuesday evening that he did not reveal his plans to introduce this resolution to Republican leadership out of concern that they would try to prevent this effort.

“I was afraid that they would do something to subvert me getting on the floor for an hour and 20 minutes and reading these articles,” he said.

Massie told Collins that he introduced the privileged resolution on Tuesday so that House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) would be forced to introduce it within the 48-hour time period before the House broke for recess.

“He could call the vote tomorrow or the day after tomorrow, and that was another reason for the timing,” Massie said on Tuesday evening. “If I were to offer this tomorrow instead of today, they could have punted this until after the election.”

The House will return following the midterm elections on Nov. 9, following Johnson’s decision to cut short the last two weeks of the September session earlier this month.

“The House has done it’s work,” Johnson told reporters after the amended schedule was released on Wednesday, according to comments shared by CBS News .

“It’s time for our members to go home to their districts and make their case to the American people, to go and explain all of the great things we’ve done,” the GOP leader said.
